title: Six faces, six mothers
hookLine: six star sisters, one hungry baby, and a god with six faces
carry: shanmukha: six faces, one for each mother
tomorrow: why would a book named for a god read like a travel guide?

lines: A BABY PASSED AROUND THE ROOM.
cards: At a family party, a newborn gets passed around the room: an aunt, a grandmother, a cousin, each one waiting for a turn.

In one old story, six women who are also stars find a baby lying in a bed of reeds by a river, and every one of them wants to nurse him. There's one baby. Then he does something no ordinary baby can do.
That's one telling of how Skanda, also called Kartikeya, came to be, and a whole Purana carries his name.

teach.h: ONLY A SON OF SHIVA CAN WIN.
teach.b: The tellings differ from text to text, but the shape is shared. The gods are in trouble. A demon, Taraka, can be beaten only by a son of Shiva, and Shiva is deep in meditation.
When the son finally comes, he comes as fire, too fierce to hold.
In several tellings it passes from Agni, the fire god, to the river Ganga, and comes to rest in a bed of reeds. There the Krittikas, star sisters, find him, and each wants to nurse him.
So he grows six faces, one for each mother, and drinks from all of them, and the story says he's called Kartikeya because of them.

teach.h: SHANMUKHA: SIX FACES FOR SIX MOTHERS.
teach.b: That's why temple images show him with six faces, and why one of his names is Shanmukha, the six-faced; as Murugan, he is loved across Tamil Nadu. He grows fast, leads the gods' army, and defeats Taraka.
Feel the story's textures: fire too hot for any hand, cool river water, soft reeds, a baby's hunger. The fire nobody can hold gets passed along, hand to hand, until it can be a child.
And the child no single mother could raise gets several, and instead of choosing, he becomes someone who can turn toward each of them.

teach.h: A FACE FOR EVERYONE WHO CARED.
teach.b: Today is the birth the Purana is named for: six faces, turned toward everyone who took care of him.

how: Kartikeya, also called Murugan, especially in Tamil-speaking regions, is shown with six faces and a spear; his birth is retold at his festivals, and the Skanda Purana carries his name.

o: a battle hymn sung before the gods' war
the Purana named for Shiva's son Skanda
a star chart naming six sisters in the sky

games.q: who's who in Kartikeya's birth — tap the pairs.
p: a demon only Shiva's son can beat
passes on the fire too fierce to hold
star sisters who nurse the baby

s: Kartikeya's six faces are for watching six directions in battle
in this telling he grows them so he can nurse from each of his six star mothers.
the tellings of his birth differ from text to text
the shape is shared: Taraka, a fierce fire, the reeds, the Krittikas.
in the story he picks one of the six to be his real mother
he doesn't choose; he turns a face toward each.

games.q: at a Murugan temple, your little cousin points at the six-faced statue: 'why does he have so many heads?' by his birth story, what do you tell him?
o: so he can watch for demons in every direction at once.
six star mothers nursed him, and he grew a face for each.
each face is a different god sharing one body.
games.why: in the birth story the Krittikas each want to nurse him, so he grows six faces. that's why he's Shanmukha, the six-faced.

practice: Sit tall, and turn your head slowly, a little to one side, then the other, then gently up and down. At each turn, bring to mind one person who helped raise you or look after you, and let your face rest toward them for a breath.
If you pray, you can thank God for each of them.

wordCard.voice: The Skanda. The Purana named for Skanda, Shiva's son, called Kartikeya after the star sisters who nursed him.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Kartikeya, the one of the Krittikas, named in the story for the star sisters who nursed him.

carryVoice: Your line: Shanmukha, six faces, one turned to each mother who came. More tomorrow.
